title: Reading the internet
objectives: Describe pretraining as learning to predict the next token of a huge body of text.

screens.prose: In ai-basics you built a next-word table from a 20-word text. Here is its row for "the". We want it to finish **the dog sat on the ...**

state.caption: The row for "the" from the 20-word text in ai-basics

screens.question: Which word does the table pick most often to come next?

options.text: cat
mat
options.why: You picked the word that fits the sentence. The table looks only at the last word, "the", and mat has 1 count in 6.

options.text: dog
options.why: Dog has 1 count in 6. The table does not know a dog is already in the sentence.

options.text: jam
options.why: Jam has 1 count in 6, the same as mat and dog. Cat has 3.

hints.text: Which count in the row is the largest?
Read the counts row.
Cat has 3 of the 6 counts, so its chance is $\tfrac36 = \tfrac12$.

feedback.correct: Cat, with chance $\tfrac12$. Half the time the table writes "the dog sat on the cat".
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the largest count in the row for "the".

explain.text: The table reads only the last word, "the", and cat follows it 3 times in 6. So it picks cat half the time, whatever came earlier in the sentence.

screens.prose: Now the same words go to a model that has read far more text than 20 words. Slide between the two charts to compare their chances for the next word.

state.caption: The 20-word table: it sees only the last word, "the". ($\tfrac16$ is drawn as 0.17.)

frames.caption: The 20-word table: it sees only the last word, "the". ($\tfrac16$ is drawn as 0.17.)
A model that has read far more text (illustrative numbers that add to 1)

screens.question: What does the model that has read far more text do differently?

options.text: It puts most of the chance on words that fit the whole sentence
It still puts the most chance on cat, as the table does
options.why: Slide to the second chart. Cat gets only 0.05 there, and mat gets 0.45.

options.text: It gives every possible next word about the same chance
options.why: The chances are far from equal: mat has 0.45 and jam has 0.

options.text: It finds the one right word and gives it all of the chance
options.why: No word gets all the chance. Several words fit, so the chance is spread over them.

hints.text: Slide to the second chart and find its tallest bar.
Compare the cat bar in the two charts.
Mat, floor and sofa take most of the chance, because a dog sits on such things.

feedback.correct: It reads every word so far, not only the last one. It has also seen a great many sentences like this.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to the second chart and see which words get the tall bars.

explain.text: The table saw 20 words and looks one word back. A model that has read a huge body of text looks at all the words so far. It has seen how such sentences usually end.

canvas.caption: A model that has read far more text (illustrative numbers that add to 1)

screens.prose: That model learned in one way only. It read a huge body of text and, at every place, tried to predict the next token. A token is a word or a piece of one, as in ai-basics. This training is called **pretraining**, and its result is a **base model**.

state.caption: Tokens so far, then the hidden next one

screens.question: During pretraining, what is the network asked to do at the hidden cell?

options.text: Predict the hidden next token
Copy the whole sentence into memory
options.why: You pictured it storing the text. It is scored only on its guess for the next token.

options.text: Decide whether the sentence is true
options.why: You gave it a truth check. Nothing in the text says true or false; only the next token is scored.

options.text: Answer a question about the fund
options.why: There is no question here. The text is just text, and the task is the next token.

hints.text: What is missing from the row?
The last cell is hidden.
Pretraining hides the next token and asks for it, at every place in the text.

feedback.correct: The real next token is the label, so every place in the text gives one example.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what is hidden in the last cell.

explain.text: Each place in the text is one example: the tokens so far are the input and the real next token is the label. Training lowers the error on these guesses, as your script in ai-basics lowered its error.

canvas.caption: Input: the tokens so far. Label: the real next token.

screens.prose: A base model has only been pretrained. It is given exactly this text and asked to go on.
screens.question: What does it most likely write next?

options.text: A likely continuation, such as "Paris.", perhaps then another "Q:"
A friendly reply: "Great question. The capital of France is Paris."
options.why: That friendly style is a habit taught later, by fine-tuning (l2). A base model only continues text.

options.text: Nothing at all, because it keeps no list of the world's capitals
options.why: It needs no list. It writes whatever text is likely to come next, and some text always is.

options.text: A refusal, because the question was not asked politely
options.why: A base model has no rules about politeness. It continues the text it is given.

hints.text: In text on the web, what usually comes after "A:"?
The model fills the next cell, then the one after.
It continues the pattern: an answer, and possibly another question and answer.

feedback.correct: After a question and "A:", text usually goes on with an answer, so a likely answer comes next. It may then carry on with another "Q:".
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A base model continues the text with what usually follows it.

explain.text: The base model treats the question as the start of a page of questions and answers. It writes what such pages usually hold next. That often looks like an answer, but only because answers follow "A:" in text.

screens.prose: Now the base model is given the start of an exam paper. You hoped it would answer the questions.

lines: 2. Explain why bond prices fall when interest rates rise.
params.title: Text given to a base model (an invented example)

screens.question: What is it most likely to write after "3."?

options.text: A third exam question
Answers to questions 1 and 2
options.why: You expected an assistant. In text, a numbered list of questions is usually followed by more questions.

options.text: A short summary of economics
options.why: Nothing in the text asks for a summary. After "3." in an exam paper comes question 3.

options.text: A note that it cannot sit exams
options.why: That is a trained assistant's kind of reply. A base model just continues the page.

hints.text: What comes after "3." on a real exam paper?
Read the last line.
The pattern of the page is a numbered list of questions, so the likely next text is question 3.

feedback.correct: An exam paper goes on with question 3, so that is the likely text.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what usually follows "3." on a page like this.

explain.text: After number 3 in an exam paper comes a third question. The base model continues the page it was given. Getting answers needs the extra training of l2.

screens.prose: In ai-basics a model was judged on questions it had not seen, and more examples helped it there. Pretraining uses the same idea at a far larger scale.
screens.question: Why does more text, with a bigger network to learn from it, usually predict the next token better?

options.text: It sees more examples of each pattern, and a bigger network can hold more of them
More text lets it store every sentence it reads and copy one out
options.why: It learns patterns that also fit sentences it never saw. That is why it can continue new text.

options.text: A big enough network trained on enough text is never wrong
options.why: You made it perfect. A bigger network predicts better on average and still gets many tokens wrong.

options.text: More text means it can check which of the facts it read are true
options.why: Text does not label facts as true. More text gives more examples of what is written, true or not.

hints.text: What did more examples do for the model in ai-basics?
Compare the counts in the middle column.
Two examples of "sat on the" give a rough guess. A great many give a much better one.

feedback.correct: More examples give better chances, and a bigger network can learn more patterns from them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of what more examples did in ai-basics.

explain.text: With 20 words, "sat on the" was seen twice; a huge body of text holds a great many such examples. So its chances rest on far more evidence. As in ai-basics, more examples help on cases not seen before.

screens.prose: Most of a model's text came in a few widely used languages. Someone asks it a question in a language that appears only rarely in that text.

columns: How much of the text it read

screens.question: What should you expect from its answer?

options.text: A weaker answer, because it saw few examples in that language
The same quality as in a common language, since the facts are the same
options.why: It learned from text, and this language gave it few examples, so its answers tend to be weaker even when the facts are the same.

options.text: No answer at all, since it cannot read the language
options.why: It will still write likely tokens. They are just less likely to be good ones.

options.text: A better answer, since rarer text is more carefully written
options.why: Fewer examples give a weaker pattern, not more care.

hints.text: How many examples did it see in that language?
Read the second row.
Few examples give weak predictions, as in ai-basics.

feedback.correct: Few examples, weaker patterns: its answers in that language tend to be worse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about how many examples it learned from in that language.

explain.text: Pretraining learns from examples, so a pattern seen rarely is learned poorly. Answers in a rare language tend to be weaker. It is the ai-basics lesson again: little data, weak predictions.

screens.prose: A friend watches a chatbot answer a question and says: "It looked the answer up in its memory of facts." The fund in this example is invented.

lines: You: When was the Larkfield Growth Fund launched?
Chatbot: The Larkfield Growth Fund was launched in 2004.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: What did the model actually do?

options.text: Wrote likely tokens one at a time; it keeps no list of facts
Looked up the launch year in a list of facts it keeps
options.why: You pictured a store of facts. The network holds numbers that make some tokens likely; there is no list to look up.

options.text: Searched the web for the fund and copied the year
options.why: Pretraining makes a predictor, not a search engine. Some chatbots are joined to a search tool, but nothing here shows one.

options.text: Wrote a year only because it was sure of the answer
options.why: It has no record of being sure to check. A year after "launched in" is simply likely text.

hints.text: What was the network trained to do in pretraining?
The year is the next token after "launched in".
It predicts likely tokens. A year is likely there, true or not.

feedback.correct: A year after "launched in" is likely text, so a year is written. Nothing checks it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the one thing pretraining trains.

byKey.lookup: You pictured a list of facts inside the network. There is none: the year is just the likely next token, which may or may not be true.

explain.text: Pretraining trains one thing: predicting the next token. A launch year is likely after "launched in", so one is written. Whether it is the true year depends on what the text taught it, and nothing checks.

screens.prose: Pretraining in one line: at every place in a huge body of text, predict the next token and lower the error. $$\text{tokens so far} \;\to\; \text{chances for the next token}$$ The result, a base model, continues the text it is given.
screens.question: Which sentence describes a base model?

options.text: It continues text with likely tokens
It answers requests like an assistant
options.why: Answering like an assistant comes from fine-tuning (l2). A base model continues text.

options.text: It looks up facts and reports them
options.why: There is no list of facts. It predicts likely tokens.

options.text: It checks whether text is true
options.why: Nothing in pretraining marks text as true or false.

feedback.correct: A base model continues text, one likely token at a time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what pretraining asks for at every place in the text.

screens.prose: An analyst at a fund types the opening of a report and lets a base model go on. They plan to paste the result into a note for clients. Firm X is invented.

lines: Analyst: Results for Firm X, third quarter. Revenue rose 8% to £412 million.
Base model: Operating profit rose 5% to £61 million. The board declared a dividend of 4.2p a share. Shares rose 3% in early trading.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Why does the paragraph read like a report, and is it safe to use?

options.text: It goes on as reports usually do, so its figures look right but are not Firm X's real results
It is a summary of Firm X's real results, so it can go into the note as it stands
options.why: You read it as a summary. The base model continued the text; the profit and dividend were never given to it.

options.text: It reads like a report because it copied Firm X's own report from its memory
options.why: It had no access to Firm X's report. It wrote what usually follows such an opening.

options.text: It is safe to use, because the first figure in it, the 8% rise, is right
options.why: Only the analyst typed the 8%. Every figure after it was written by the model and is unchecked.

hints.text: Which figures did the analyst type, and which did the model write?
The second line is all model text.
A base model continues a report in the style of reports. Its numbers are likely-looking, not looked up.

feedback.correct: It reads like a report because it continues one. Its figures are likely-looking, so each must be checked before a client sees it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate what the analyst typed from what the model wrote.

explain.text: The model continued the document in the style of results reports. The profit, dividend and share move are likely-looking numbers, not facts about Firm X. Each one must be checked before it reaches a client.

ideas: Pretraining shows a network a huge body of text and asks it, at every place, for the next token. The text supplies its own labels.
The result is a base model: it continues the text it is given with likely tokens. More text and a bigger network usually predict better.
A base model keeps no list of facts to look up. A name or a number it writes is likely text, which may or may not be true.

formula.name: Pretraining
formula.tex: \text{tokens so far} \to \text{chances for the next token}
formula.note: The real next token in the text is the label.

summary.trap: "It looked the answer up" is wrong. A model predicts likely tokens, and nothing checks them.

quiz.question: In pretraining, where do the labels come from?

options.text: The text itself: each next token is a label
People mark each sentence true or false
options.why: Nobody marks the text. The next token in the text is the label.

options.text: People write an answer to each question
options.why: Answers written by people are used later, in fine-tuning (l2).

options.text: The network makes up its own labels
options.why: The network guesses; the text holds the real next token to score the guess.

feedback.correct: The text supplies its own labels: each next token.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is hidden and then scored in pretraining.

explain.text: Pretraining hides the next token at every place in the text and scores the guess against it. So the text supplies every label, and no person has to write one.

quiz.question: A base model is given: "Dear customer, we are sorry to tell you that". What does it do?

options.text: Continues the letter with likely words
Asks who the customer is
options.why: Asking questions back is an assistant's habit. A base model continues the text.

options.text: Refuses, since no question was asked
options.why: A base model needs no question. It continues whatever text it is given.

options.text: Checks whether the bad news is true
options.why: There is nothing to check against. It writes likely text.

feedback.correct: It continues the letter, as letters like it usually go on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A base model only continues text.

explain.text: The text looks like the start of a letter, so the likely next words continue the letter. That is all a base model does.

quiz.question: Two models are pretrained in the same way. One reads ten times as much text. On new text neither has seen, which tends to predict the next token better?

options.text: The one that read more text
Both the same, since the method is the same
options.why: The method is the same, but one learned from far more examples.

options.text: The one that read less, as it is less confused
options.why: More examples sharpen the patterns; they do not confuse them.

options.text: Neither can predict text it has not seen
options.why: Predicting unseen text is the point. As in ai-basics, a model is judged on cases it has not seen.

feedback.correct: More text, more examples of each pattern, better predictions on new text.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of what more examples did in ai-basics.

explain.text: With the same method, more text gives more examples of each pattern. That usually means better predictions on text neither model has seen.

quiz.question: A chatbot with no search tool gives the number of shops a retailer owns. How did it produce the number?

options.text: It wrote a number that is likely text in that place
It counted the shops in a list it keeps
options.why: There is no list to count. The number is likely text.

options.text: It asked the retailer
options.why: A model on its own contacts no one. It predicts tokens.

options.text: It wrote the true number, as it only writes facts
options.why: It writes likely text, which may or may not be the true number.

feedback.correct: A likely number, not a looked-up one. It may or may not be right.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what pretraining trains.

explain.text: The model predicts likely tokens, and a number is likely after such a question. Whether it is right depends on what the text taught it, so it needs checking.
